citation: Zhang Z, Qu W, Peng W, Sun J, Yue J, Guan L, Lu M, Li D (2025). Effect of unilateral and bilateral plyometric training on jumping, sprinting, and change of direction abilities: a meta-analysis. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation.
population: 328 healthy participants (31.7% male, 49.4% female, 18.9% sex not reported) aged 9–65 years, including pre-adolescents (9–12 years), youth (13–18 years), and adults (18–65 years) from sports such as volleyball, basketball, badminton, soccer, and recreational to professional levels.
intervention: Unilateral plyometric training (experimental) vs bilateral plyometric training (control); sessions 20–90 min, 2–3 times/week over 6–12 weeks; exercises included single-leg jumps, depth jumps, hurdle jumps, box jumps, squat jumps, countermovement jumps, sprints, broad jumps, and agility drills.
outcome_measures: change of direction ability (seconds, T-agility test, 505 test)
summary: This meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (328 healthy participants) compared unilateral versus bilateral plyometric training. Unilateral training significantly improved single-leg jump performance (ES = 0.29) and vertical jump performance (ES = 0.53), while bilateral training was superior for bilateral jump performance (ES = -0.07). Unilateral training also significantly enhanced sprint performance (ES = -0.04) and change of direction ability (ES = -0.07). Low ground contact frequency (<900 total contacts) significantly enhanced vertical jump performance (ES = 0.64).
key_findings: Unilateral training improved single-leg jump performance more than bilateral training (ES = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.06–0.52; Z = 2.46, p = 0.01).
No significant difference between unilateral and bilateral training for double-leg jump performance (ES = -0.07, 95% CI: -0.23–0.09; Z = 0.88, p = 0.38).
Unilateral training significantly improved vertical jump performance versus control (ES = 0.53, 95% CI: 0.02–1.04; Z = 2.05, p = 0.04).
Low ground contact frequency (<900 contacts) significantly enhanced vertical jump performance (ES = 0.64, 95% CI: 0.01–1.27; Z = 2.00, p = 0.05).

Unilateral training significantly improved sprint performance (ES = -0.04, 95% CI: -0.07 to -0.01; Z = 2.32, p = 0.02) and change of direction ability (ES = -0.07, 95% CI: -0.12 to -0.03; Z = 3.29, p = 0.001).
Bilateral training showed greater effect on bilateral jump performance (ES = -0.07, 95% CI: -0.12 to -0.03; Z = 3.39, p = 0.0007).
effect_size: ES = 0.29 (single-leg jump), ES = 0.53 (vertical jump), ES = 0.64 (LGCF vertical jump), ES = -0.04 (sprint), ES = -0.07 (COD), ES = -0.07 (bilateral jump favoring BI)
limitations: Moderate heterogeneity (I² = 49%) in vertical jump analysis; subgroup analyses limited by few studies per category; mixed population across youth to adults with 18.9% sex not reported; only 11 studies met inclusion criteria, some subgroups had <2 studies and were excluded.
